item.title: Tektronix 1 Series low-cost DPO oscilloscopes support AI-assisted control, start at just $450
item.dc:creator: Debashis Das
item.description:
Tektronix is better known for its high-end and pricey oscilloscopes, but has now introduced the 1 Series DPO, a line of low-cost digital phosphor oscilloscopes starting at just $450, with optional AI-assisted control through the new Tek Intelligence connector. These oscilloscopes are designed for electronics testing, embedded development, education, and everyday circuit debugging. The 1 Series DPOs feature up to four analog channels, 50 MHz to 200 MHz bandwidth, 12-bit vertical resolution, and up to 1.25 GS/s sampling rate. They also integrate a 7-inch touchscreen and 10 Mpoints of memory per channel, support I2C, SPI, and UART protocol decoding, and implement built-in waveform analysis tools. The higher-priced S models add a 25 MHz arbitrary function generator (AFG) and Bode plot analysis. Tektronix 1 Series DPO key specifications: Models – 16 variants covering four bandwidth options, two channel configurations, and versions with or without AFG Display – 7-inch capacitive multi-touchscreen, 1024 [...]

item.title: Home Assistant-compatible ESP32 4-channel PWM fan controller is designed for server racks and NAS systems
item.dc:creator: Debashis Das
item.description:
Designed by CoolMaker Lab in China, the ESP32 4-channel PWM fan controller is an open-source, Home Assistant-compatible board for managing cooling in server racks, NAS systems, network cabinets, and other DIY enclosures. It can independently control up to four 4-pin PWM fans, supporting PWM-based speed adjustment, tachometer-based RPM monitoring, and individual fan power switching. The controller supports up to four external DS18B20 temperature sensors for automatic fan speed adjustment, along with a web interface, an HTTP REST API, and Bluetooth proxy functionality. The latest v2.0 hardware and firmware also support optional LD2402G 24GHz mmWave radar for presence-based automation. item.title: HIYD ultrathin health tracker attaches to the back of regular watches (Crowdfunding)
item.dc:creator: Debashis Das
item.description:
HIYD is a compact and thin (2.7mm) health and fitness tracker that attaches to the back of a regular wristwatch and looks very similar to the Azume One, which we wrote about last month.  Developed by San Jose-based HIYD, the device adds heart rate, sleep, recovery, and activity tracking to traditional watches using a removable microsuction mechanism. It features optical sensors for heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV), and blood oxygen (SpO2) monitoring, along with an accelerometer and skin temperature sensor. The device connects to Android and iOS smartphones over Bluetooth and supports sleep tracking, daily readiness scores, and camera-based nutrition logging. Battery life is rated at up to four days and can be extended to 20 days with an optional battery band, with no subscription fees for Kickstarter backers. item.title: Lumissil IS31CS9202/IS32CS9202 Cortex-M0+ MCUs integrate serial video bus (SBV), LumiBus, and capacitive touch-key controller
item.dc:creator: Jean-Luc Aufranc (CNXSoft)
item.description:
Lumissil Microsystems IS31CS9202 and IS32CS9202 are 50 MHz Cortex-M0+ microcontrollers for industrial, consumer, and automotive applications with a serial video bus (SVB), a LumiBus LED controller, and a capacitive touch-key controller. Both chips come with 16KB RAM, 256KB flash, a CAN FD controller, SPI master/slave, I2C master/slave, two enhanced UART interfaces, a quadrature encoder, a 14-bit sigma-delta ADC, a 12-bit SAR ADC, an 8-bit DAC, up to 42 GPIO pins, and more. The only differences are that the IS32CS9202 is designed for automotive applications and benefits from a wider -40°C to 125°C temperature range and AEC-Q100 and ASIL-B qualifications. Lumissil IS31CS9202/IS32CS9202 key features and specifications: CPU – Arm Cortex-M0+ core up to 50MHz Memory – 16KB RAM with ECC 8KB for data memory 8KB for DMA memory Storage  256KB flash with four 1KB IFBs (Information Blocks) with ECC Data flash emulation 1K/ 10K/100K cycles endurance @ 125, 105, 85°C 10 [...]

item.title: Mikrotik KNOT Gateway HL9 – An outdoor Wi-Fi HaLow IoT gateway with GbE, WiFi 6, BLE 5.1, 4G LTE Cat 1 bis, and GNSS
item.dc:creator: Debashis Das
item.description:
MikroTik KNOT Gateway HL9 is an IP66-rated outdoor IoT gateway that combines 915 MHz Wi-Fi HaLow (802.11ah), Bluetooth 5.1, Wi-Fi 6, LTE Cat 1 bis, Gigabit Ethernet, and GNSS. The gateway supports asset tracking, remote sensor monitoring, industrial IoT, and agricultural applications. Built around a dual-core Qualcomm IPQ-5010 ARM64 processor, it features 256MB RAM and 128MB NAND flash. It relies on a Morse Micro MM6108 Wi-Fi HaLow SoC for sub-GHz connectivity, with Gigabit Ethernet, 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi 6, and LTE Cat 1 bis cellular for backhaul. item.title: Renesas RZ/T2N Cortex-A55/R52 industrial MPU supports four-axis motor control, TSN Ethernet, EtherCAT…
item.dc:creator: Debashis Das
item.description:
Renesas RZ/T2N industrial MPU supports up to four-axis motor control and includes PWM timers, encoder interfaces, and trigonometric accelerators. It’s designed for industrial robots, programmable logic controllers (PLCs), motion controllers, and multi-axis servo drives. The MPU features up to two 1.2 GHz Arm Cortex-A55 cores for application processing and two 800 MHz Cortex-R52 cores for real-time control. It also integrates a three-port Gigabit Ethernet switch with TSN support and industrial Ethernet protocols such as EtherCAT, PROFINET RT/IRT, and EtherNet/IP. This feature set allows real-time motor control, industrial networking, and Linux applications to run on a single chip, reducing the need for separate processors. The MPU can also work as an industrial Ethernet network controller or device, depending on the application. item.title: LocalDot – Open-source PCB for 3rd-gen Amazon Echo Dot enables Home Assistant support (Crowdfunding)
item.dc:creator: Debashis Das
item.description:
AAElectronics’ LocalDot is an open-source replacement mainboard that converts a 3rd-generation Amazon Echo Dot into a local voice assistant compatible with Home Assistant. The board replaces one of the two original PCBs while reusing the existing microphones, speaker, buttons, LEDs, and enclosure, so the device works without relying on Amazon’s cloud services. The board combines an ESP32-S3 for WiFi connectivity and device control with an ESP32-P4 for audio processing. It supports the original four-microphone array with beamforming, on-device wake-word detection, and local voice commands through Home Assistant. Installation requires no soldering or enclosure modifications, and the device still uses the original Echo Dot power adapter. LocalDot specifications: Compatibility – 3rd-generation Amazon Echo Dot (Donut and Crumpet variants; Clock version not tested) SoC ESP32-S3 – Wi-Fi connectivity and device control ESP32-P4 – Dedicated audio processing Audio TAS5805 audio amplifier for the original speaker On-device wake-word detection Beamforming support Reuses the original [...]

item.title: LabWired allows engineers to test compiled firmware on simulated MCU boards (CPU and peripherals)
item.dc:creator: Jean-Luc Aufranc (CNXSoft)
item.description:
Andrii Shylenko’s LabWired is an MIT-licensed MCU firmware simulation core that runs compiled firmware against modeled CPUs and peripherals, captures UART and bus output, register state, and supports repeatable checks in CI. The simulator works on Arm Cortex-M0+, Cortex-M3, Cortex-M4, Cortex-M7, Cortex-M33 cores, RISC-V architecutre, and Xtensa LX6 and LX7 (some ESP32 parts). The main benefit of the project is speeding up firmware testing since doing some on real boards is slow. The hardware must be ready, then the firmware must be flashed to the board each time you want to test it, and if something breaks, developers get a dark LED and no trace. If a firmware project needs to support multiple boards, this quickly adds up. The project is different from a CPU/MCU emulator for two main reasons: The full board is modeled, not only the chip. Sensors, displays, and bus devices are also simulated. So you can [...]

item.title: KiCad 10 now (unofficially) runs in a web browser or Android
item.dc:creator: Jean-Luc Aufranc (CNXSoft)
item.description:
It’s now possible to run KiCad 10 directly in a web browser or as an Android app thanks to two separate open-source projects, unaffiliated with the official KiCad project. Let’s have a look at both. Ziro Designer/ZiroEDA – KiCad 10 in your web browser Akshay Rukade (ZiroEDA), an engineering student in India, ported KiCad 10.0.6 to the browser through the Ziro Designer/ZiroEDA Designer project. It’s a TypeScript translation of KiCad’s C++, kept file-for-file against the KiCad implementation, so the real schematic editor, PCB editor, interactive router, and ERC/DRC run in a browser tab and read and write normal KiCad projects. That means you can open local KiCad projects or designs hosted on GitHub directly in a web browser without having to install KiCad 10 itself on your computer, and it should also enable machines that do not natively support KiCad (e.g., RISC-V, Android tablet, iPad…) to run it. Akshay highlights [...]

item.title: ControlBox Home Assistant solution is designed for floor heating systems, house lighting, 1-wire sensors (Crowdfunding)
item.dc:creator: Jean-Luc Aufranc (CNXSoft)
item.description:
DomeCtrl’s ControlBox is a Raspberry Pi 5-based controller running Home Assistant and primarily designed for hydronic radiant floor heating (RFH) systems. It also supports lighting solutions and integration with energy devices such as solar collectors, photovoltaic installations, heat pumps, hydraulic pumps & valves. The system controls thermal valves, hydraulic PWM pumps, and related RFH devices, and can read multiple 1-wire temperature sensors over long cables (>6 m).  The ControlBox also features 32 LED-strip output channels, for up to 2 kW output. item.title: 280 MHz STMicro STM32G5 Cortex-M33 mixed-signal MCU targets digital power and motor control applications
item.dc:creator: Debashis Das
item.description:
The STM32G5 series is a family of 280 MHz Arm Cortex-M33 mixed-signal MCUs designed for industrial power supplies, photovoltaic inverters, EV chargers, robotics, and motor control systems. It doubles the performance of the older STM32G4 series unveiled in 2021. The new MCU family features up to 512KB flash, 112KB SRAM with ECC, a 111 ps high-resolution timer (HRTIM) with up to 12 PWM outputs on some variants, and 12-bit ADCs supporting up to 5 MSPS. Other features include position encoder interfaces, a 16-element programmable logic array, CORDIC and FMAC mathematical accelerators, and security features such as Arm TrustZone, secure boot, and post-quantum cryptography support. STM32G5 series specifications: MCU Core 32-bit Arm Cortex-M33 CPU @ up to 280 MHz with TrustZone, single-precision FPU, DSP instructions, and MPU 8 KB instruction cache and 4 KB data cache (data cache on STM32G55x/56x only) 20 KB or 32 KB CCM-SRAM routine booster (20 KB [...]

item.title: Seeed Studio XIAO STM32C5 development board features dual CAN FD and a 6-axis IMU with programmable heating
item.dc:creator: Debashis Das
item.description:
Seeed Studio XIAO STM32C5 is the company’s first XIAO development board based on an STMicroelectronics MCU, namely a 144 MHz STM32C5A3CG Arm Cortex-M33 microcontroller. It features two CAN FD controllers and a 6-axis IMU with programmable heating for robotics, industrial control, and motion-sensing applications. The board also includes 16MB of external flash, a 48 MHz external crystal, a USB-C port, and battery charging circuitry. One CAN FD channel is connected to an onboard transceiver, while the second requires an external transceiver. The integrated IMU heater allows firmware to control sensor temperature and reduce measurement drift from temperature changes. item.title: SparkFun IoT RedBoard ESP32-P4 – Arduino UNO-like ESP32-P4 v3.x development boards with WiFi 6 or PoE options
item.dc:creator: Debashis Das
item.description:
SparkFun introduced two new development boards called IoT RedBoard, both based on the ESP32-P4 v3.x (ESP32-P4X) and compatible with the Arduino UNO R3 form factor. The main difference is that one features an ESP32-C5 for Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5 LE, Zigbee, and Thread connectivity, while the PoE version includes 10/100 Mbps Ethernet and Power over Ethernet (PoE) support. They also include MIPI CSI/DSI camera and display connectors, two USB-C ports, a microSD card slot, Qwiic expansion, Arduino R3-compatible headers, and LiPo battery charging and monitoring. These features make it suitable for HMI, edge computing, and IoT applications. M5Stack’s Core Matrix is an ESP32-C61-based IoT controller with a 16×16 white LED matrix for displaying icons, animations, device status, and notifications. item.title: Waveshare ESP32-S31-Zero – A tiny ESP32-S31 board with up to 32MB PSRAM, 32MB SPI flash
item.dc:creator: Jean-Luc Aufranc (CNXSoft)
item.description:
Waveshare ESP32-S31-Zero is a small ESP32-S31 development board that follows the form factor of the earlier Waveshare “Zero” boards, such as the ESP32-C6-Zero-B, RA4M1-Zero, and ESP32-S3-Zero, among others. The new tiny board still features a USB-C port for power and programming, as well as eighteen through and castellated holes for GPIO and power signals,  but it boasts a more powerful ESP32-S31 dual-core RISC-V MCU clocked at up to 320 MHz, featuring 2.4 GHz WiFi 6, Bluetooth 5.3, and 802.15.4 connectivity, as well as up to 32MB on-chip PSRAM and a 16MB or 32MB SPI flash chip. Since the ESP32-S31 has quite a few extra I/Os, Waveshare also added a 40-pin high-density connector for LCD, touchscreen, SD card, USB 2.0, and extra GPIOs. item.title: 520 MHz STM32H7P4/STM32H7P5 Arm Cortex-M7 MCUs feature Hardware Signal Processor (HSP), optional Neural-ART NPU
item.dc:creator: Debashis Das
item.description:
STMicroelectronics has introduced the STM32H7P4 and STM32H7P5, two 520 MHz Arm Cortex-M7 MCUs part of STM32H7P family designed for digital power, motor control, industrial sensing, and edge AI applications. Both feature a Hardware Signal Processor (HSP) for accelerating mathematical and signal-processing operations, while the STM32H7P5 also includes an 85 GOPS Neural-ART NPU for Edge AI inference/TinyML. The MCUs feature up to 2MB dual-bank flash, 736KB SRAM, two high-resolution timers with up to 24 PWM outputs, three advanced motor-control timers, and four 12-bit ADCs. Other features include CORDIC and FMAC mathematical accelerators, three CAN FD interfaces, USB OTG Full-Speed, and support for external memory through Octo-SPI and FMC interfaces. item.title: Olimex UEXT-CH390 SPI to Ethernet module targets Raspberry Pi and ESP32 MCU boards running ESPHome
item.dc:creator: Debashis Das
item.description:
Olimex UEXT-CH390 is a small open-source hardware module that adds 10/100 Mbps wired Ethernet connectivity to microcontroller boards through an SPI interface. It is designed for Raspberry Pi Pico and Pico 2 boards, as well as ESP32-S3, C3, C5, C6, and other microcontrollers without built-in Ethernet connectivity. The module is based on the WCH CH390 Ethernet controller and features an RJ45 connector, a standard UEXT connector, and a smaller 1.0mm-pitch pUEXT connector. It measures 50 x 21 mm and is supported in the Arduino IDE and ESPHome firmware, making it suitable for wired IoT sensors, Home Assistant devices, and other applications where WiFi is unreliable or unwanted. item.title: NXP MCX W70 and KW43 wireless MCUs support Bluetooth Channel Sounding for IoT and automotive applications
item.dc:creator: Debashis Das
item.description:
NXP MCX W70 and KW43 wireless MCU families support Bluetooth 6.x Channel Sounding for secure distance measurement in industrial IoT and automotive applications. The MCX W70 supports Bluetooth LE, Zigbee, Thread, and Matter for Smart Home and industrial devices, while the KW43 is designed for automotive applications such as digital keys and secure vehicle access. Both families feature a 96 MHz Arm Cortex-M33 application core, a separate Cortex-M33 core for wireless connectivity, up to 1.5MB flash, 256KB SRAM, a dedicated Localization Compute Engine (LCE), and NXP’s EdgeLock security features. item.title: P4 Launcher offers a PC-like and retro gaming experience on ESP32-P4 boards
item.dc:creator: Jean-Luc Aufranc (CNXSoft)
item.description:
Gil Tal has developed the P4 Launcher, an open-source application platform designed to bring a PC-like experience to ESP32-P4 boards with an attached touchscreen display. The launcher boots directly into its interface, while applications (.papp files) are stored on a microSD card and loaded into PSRAM when launched. You can add, remove, and run applications without reflashing the firmware or rebooting the device by simply copying files to the microSD card.Gil says 21 PAPP (PSRAM APP) applications are available now, mostly emulators and games, including Neo Geo and Atari 2600 emulators, Doom, Quake, Duke Nukem 3D and OpenTyrian, plus Clock and Files. Like ESPBrookesia, the P4 Launcher user interface runs on ESP32-P4, but it’s more flexible since it supports apps stored on the microSD card and targets mainly gaming for now.
